(p. 396) Surat Qaf, also called al-Basiqat (The Towering Palms).

Its central aim is to confirm the Prophet (ﷺ) in his message, the greatest part of which is warning, and the greatest of its warnings is the announcement of the Day of Emergence (yawm al-khuruj). This is shown after the audible verses, whose inimitability makes them self-sufficient, by visible signs that decisively demonstrate comprehensiveness in all attributes of perfection. Better than this, it may be said: its aim is to demonstrate the all-encompassing power, which is the result of what the Chambers (al-Hujurat) concluded with, namely the all-encompassing knowledge. This demonstrates that resurrection for the Day of Threat (yawm al-wa'id) is necessary. This comprehensiveness thus embraces what results of grace among the servants with justice, because that is the secret of existence, and that is the result of the aim of al-Baqarah. What has been established to demonstrate all of this is the observed comprehensiveness of the glory [majd] of the Qur'an in its inimitability: its reaching the highest level in every one of its meanings, the elevation of its composition, the sublimity of its vocabulary, the interconnection of its letters, the harmony of its arrangement, the grace of its combinations, and the sweetness of its distinction, to a degree the powers cannot bear. It is also shown by the comprehensiveness of the attributes of the Messenger whom He chose to convey this Book to creation, and by the observed comprehensiveness of power in what the Qur'an guides to, the signs of origination (al-ijad) and annihilation (al-i'dam). Both of these possibilities are indicated by its name, Qaf, because its verses establish glory through this Book. Glory is nobility, generosity, (p. 397) elevation, and loftiness, and this cannot be unless the one who brings it is likewise, and it is inseparable from the truthfulness of everything he brought. The letter Qaf alone has the most complete indication of this. First, by its place of articulation: it comes from the root of the tongue, adjacent to the throat, facing the upper palate. This is an indication that the aim of the surah is origin and height. Each of these also indicates truthfulness with strong indication, since the original function of a report is truth, and its indication of falsehood is by convention, not by reason. Moreover, it encompasses its name or its named referent through its three places of articulation. Encompassing the truth is possible only with height, and height is possible only with truthfulness. For its encompassing, the mountain that surrounds the earth was named after it (Qaf). This is regarding its place of articulation. As for its attributes, it is great in this respect: it has jahr (audibility), shiddah (strength), infitah (openness), isti'la' (elevation), and qalqalah (vibration). Each of these clearly indicates this to a great degree. The most indicative of this aim among created things is the palm tree, because it is distinguished from other plants by its encompassing height and abundant benefits. It combines fruit for enjoyment: first the qalb (the heart of the palm, its tender core), then the tal' (the spathe), then the busr (unripe dates), then the rutab (ripe dates). It serves for sustenance with dates, for wood and firewood, for qata (its fronds), for khus (palm leaves) useful for spreading, and for fiber useful for ropes, and below these and higher than them, khilal (palm stalks used as skewers). This is in addition to the Arabs' close familiarity with it, as they are the first to whom this Book was addressed, and their knowledge of its properties. The most indicative of it is its height, although its roots lack the spread and firmness of other plants' roots. Such a thing is not normally sufficient to keep it from falling, to bear heavy loads, to endure great destruction, and to hold clustered fruit. For this reason the surah was named "The Towering Palms" (al-Basiqat), not "The Palm."

(p. 398) "In the name of God," whose encompassing praise is manifest in what His Prophet (ﷺ) has of the encompassing praise, and whose power, may He be exalted, has an encompassing that has no limit. "The Most Merciful" (al-Rahman), who encompassed His creation with His mercy when He sent Muhammad (ﷺ) to them with His laws. He is the most truthful of servants, and through the greatness of His miracles He showed that His power has no end. "The Most Compassionate" (al-Rahim), who singled out for success in the abode of permanence those who dwell in ease.

* *

When He, may He be exalted, concluded the Chambers with the comprehensiveness of knowledge, He began this surah with: ﴿Qaf﴾, indicating that He alone, may He be exalted, encompasses in knowledge and power, by what He has of elevation, strength, self-subsisting power (al-qayyumiyyah), dominance, the executing of decree, and the opening of what He wills of closed things. This is what the letter Qaf indicates by its attributes and shows by its place of articulation, which encompasses what its referent comprises of the three places of articulation: the throat, the tongue, and the lips.

Al-Ustadh Abu al-Hasan al-Harrali (d. 638 AH/1240 CE) has said, regarding the secret of beginning the mufassal (the short surahs from Qaf to the end of the Book) with this letter, at the end of his book on this letter: Know that the Qur'an was sent down as mathani (repeated/paired), except for the mufassal from it, which is from Qaf to the end of the Glorious Book, and the opening of that which pertains to people of knowledge and understanding: the expanded wisdoms, the decisive rulings, the lengthy narratives, and the ambiguous verses; and the surah opened with the universal letters for the comprehensiveness of the unseen (al-ghaybiyyah) of the spelled letters (al-mutahajji), attributed to individual numbers. Because of the high rank of its revelation and its length, the Truth, may He be exalted, divided the address and arranged it into many surahs of few verses and short in extent. In them He mentioned fragments of stories, admonitions, rulings, praise, and the matter of recompense, which suit the hearing of the common people, so that their hearing would be easy for them (p. 399), and so that they may take a share of what the elite have taken, and so that, in the recitation of the imams in the obligatory prayers, which they cannot avoid, it would be repeated in their ears as a substitute for what sustains them from the content of the rest of the lengthy surahs. Thus, the most appropriate way to open their mufassal was with the letter Qaf, which is the odd number of the units (wutr al-ahad). Its apparent content is the content of what it contains, from among those opened with Alif Lam Mim. Likewise, the Prophet (ﷺ) used to recite it often in the Friday sermon to them, because it is a comprehensive prayer (salah jami'ah) in its outward form, with the opening of the mufassal specific to them. Its content includes the meaning of power and dominance needed for establishing the affairs of the common people, which is sufficient. It was paired with the surah of al-Muthahhirah, so they were singled out for what contains dominance and turning in repentance (al-inabah). The surah of Nun was abbreviated from the requirement of knowledge with what encompasses the affairs of the common people, which ends in the goal of the Remembrance that comprises all the worlds.

Since all the surahs opened with the letters contain the nine levels and the tenth which gathers them, in sustenance and comprehensiveness throughout the whole Qur'an, the surah of Qaf and the surah of Nun have a particular sustenance and a particular comprehensiveness regarding what pertains specifically to the common people of the Qur'an, who are gathered by the earth. It encompasses its outer surface with the form of the mountain of Qaf, and what encompasses its inner part with the form of the animal of Nun, through which the completion of their affairs is by what lies between the two supports of its establishment. With this surah opened by the letter, the particularity of the Qur'an and its distinction from all other books became manifest, because it includes the comprehensiveness that is found only in the sealing and gathering. There came with it, in its surahs, an excellence appropriate to its comprehensiveness. Because of the comprehensiveness of its meanings (p. 400) and their completeness, whatever meaning is explained for it returns to its content. It is therefore correct in its comprehensiveness and its place among the names of God and their order in all the worlds. No commentator errs regarding it in this respect, because whenever he intends an aspect of interpretation, he does not go outside the comprehensiveness of what it requires. Whatever it is explained as being, whether [that they are] among the names of God, or among the names of the angels, or among the names of the prophets, or of similar things and forms of existents, or that they are oaths God swore by, or openings by which surahs are identified, or numbers indicating events and portions of outward or inward matters, according to differing ranks and states, of what was given to Muhammad (ﷺ) in terms of the extent of the caliphate, kingship, and sovereignty, and what his affair leads to of the manifestation of guidance and the like, which encompasses the extent of his day, and to other things: all of these fall within its comprehensiveness. For this reason also, it does not belong to a particular place that requires a particular sign of i'rab (grammatical inflection). Whatever is assigned to its positions in this surah, whether jarr, nasb, or raf', is included within the comprehensiveness of its rank, and no particular meaning or particular i'rab is necessary for it, since it has no syntactic connection. They are independent, comprehensive units. Connection occurs only in what makes the meaning of each of the connected parts complete through the occurrence of connection. This applies to words that fall short of the comprehensiveness of the content of letters. Thus, whenever independence and comprehensiveness occur in a word (p. 401), no connection occurs in it.

When He, may He be exalted, indicated this comprehensiveness with Qaf, He swore an oath to it, which by itself indicates it. He said: ﴿By the Qur'an﴾, meaning the gathering, distinguishing Book, ﴿the Glorious﴾, which has elevation, nobility, generosity, and greatness above every speech. The answer [to the oath] is that they know what Qaf indicates of My strength, My greatness, the comprehensiveness of My knowledge and My power, and what the Qur'an contains of glory through its inimitability and its inclusion of all greatness. They did not deny any of that in their hearts. As for the glory of the Qur'an, as was mentioned earlier in the course of al-Fatihah, you have tested its rulings from what is hastily witnessed to what is deferred yet known by knowledge of what is witnessed. It was known by the certain experience of what has been transmitted in past stories and what is witnessed in present traces, and what recurs with the passing of time of similar and comparable things. If you reflect upon the surah, you will find its verses descended upon all of this, for He, may He be exalted, reminded them [therein] of what they know of the creation of the heavens and the earth [and what is between them], and of the fates of the former peoples. The preceding surah is likewise, especially its end, which points to the fact that He brought faith among people through one man whom He overpowered with his glory and his inimitability, by the glory of the One who sent him down, through His power and the comprehensiveness of His knowledge. And God is the Guide. Whoever comprehends its meanings in knowledge and acts upon what is in it is glorified with God and with people.

(p. 402) Abu Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr said: Since the surah of al-Fath contained a group of the gentle kindnesses with which God singled out His believing servants, such as His mention of their brotherhood, and His command to them to be steadfast in the face of the danger of a transgressing sinner, ﴿O you who believe, if a deviator brings you a report﴾ [al-Hujurat: 6], and so on. He commanded them to lower their voices before their Prophet, not to put themselves forward before him, and not to deal with him in speech loudly as some of them dealt with others. He commanded them to avoid much suspicion and forbade them from spying and backbiting. He commanded them to humility in His words: ﴿O mankind, We created you from male and female﴾ [al-Hujurat: 13]. He informed them, may He be exalted, that their compliance and their carrying out of these commands were not by their own power, but by His grace and bounty. He said: ﴿But God has endeared to you faith and made it pleasing in your hearts, and He has made hateful to you disbelief, defiance, and disobedience﴾ [al-Hujurat: 7], the two verses. Then He followed that with His words: ﴿They consider it a favor to you that they have accepted Islam﴾ [al-Hujurat: 17], and so on, to make clear that all of this is in His hand and from His side. He showed them the state of one whom He decreed disbelief upon, and did not make faith beloved to him nor adorn it in his heart. Rather, He placed him at one extreme of the state of those whom He commanded and forbade in the surah of al-Hujurat, despite equality in creation and similarity of instruments. So He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿By the Glorious Qur'an﴾ [Qaf: 1], ﴿But they wonder that a warner has come to them from among themselves﴾ [Qaf: 2], and the verses after it. Then He, may He be exalted and high, mentioned the clarity of the proofs: ﴿Have they not looked at the sky above them?﴾ [Qaf: 6], and the verses. Then He mentioned the state of others who held their opinion: ﴿The people of Noah denied before them﴾ [Qaf: 12], so that by the combination of all this, the one whose mention was previously made would take heed of his state (p. 403) and his command and prohibition in the surah of al-Hujurat, and so that the believer would be disciplined by the disciplines of God, and know that whatever good befalls him is from the bounty and kindness of his Lord. Then the verses are joined up to His words at the end of the surah: ﴿We know best what they say, and you are not over them a compeller﴾ [Qaf: 45], and the verses. End.

[p. 404] Since this was evident from what the context (*siyaq*) indicates, he built on it another proof of the comprehensiveness of His knowledge: ﴿Nay, rather﴾, that is, their denial is not due to denying any part of His glory, nor to denying your truthfulness, which is part of His glory. Rather, ﴿they wondered﴾, that is, the disbelievers. He mentioned them by pronoun before any explicit mention to indicate that when He mentions something outside the norms of uprightness, He turns to them. Wonder is the mind's reaction to something outside the customary course [of affairs].

Since the situation called for frightening those who had put forward [something] before the Messenger of God (ﷺ), or had been favoured by him with Islam, or others, or for frightening those who denied the Resurrection, He limited Himself to warning and said: ﴿that a warner has come to them﴾, who warned them with the full warning of God's punishment at the Resurrection, which is the focus of wisdom. He expressed their wonder with the words ﴿from among them﴾, because the custom among them and among all people is that when the warner is one of their own, no doubt about his warning enters their minds in any way. These people, however, went against the custom of people in their wonder that the warner, who is one of them, was singled out for the message over them, and they did not grasp the reason for this particularity given that he was like them. Likewise, they denied his message and the excellence of his Book out of their own spite and envy, because they had acknowledged his qualities by which God had raised him above them before the message. Their vanity brought them down to the lowest depths of foolishness and levity of minds, for they wondered that the Messenger was a human being, and yet they deemed it fitting that God should be a stone. They wondered that they should be brought back from dust and that life should be restored to them, yet they did not wonder that they had been originated from dust, which had no origin in life. For this reason He connected to it His words: ﴿so the disbelievers said﴾, that is, because of his warning about the Resurrection and its consequence, and He used the explicit term in the place of the pronoun to signal that nothing about his affair was hidden from them, but they concealed it out of transgression, while their minds, which clearly indicate all his affair, were before their eyes. He expressed it with what indicates warning, because it is the greatest aim of this surah, and the entire context of al-Hujurat points to it: ﴿This is a strange thing﴾, namely that the warner should be one of us and be singled out for the message above us, and that what he warned of, the Resurrection after death, should be [such that], ﴿it is a strange thing﴾, that is, extremely remote from the customs of its kind. They lied in this, for as for the warner, most messengers came from the communities to which they were sent, and few were strangers to those to whom they were sent. As for the Resurrection, most of what exists in the cosmos is similar to it: the return of each of the two alternating ones (night and day) after its departure, the revival of the earth after its death, the beginning of life for all dead animal life, and the bringing forth of plants, trees and fruits, and other things that are [themselves] very evident. [p. 405]

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 50, verse 3:

When the matter they marvelled at was stated in general terms, he clarified it with his words, relating it from them as they went to great lengths in denial, opening their denial with an interrogative of denial: ﴿When we are dead and have become dust?﴾ That is, when our spirits have departed from our bodies and we have become dust, with no distinction between it and the dust of the earth. And since the element governing the adverbial phrase (al-'amil fi al-zarf) had an implied estimate, namely "we will return?", he indicated it by his words, and by the demonstrative particle of distance, to the greatness of their considering it remote: ﴿That﴾, i.e., the matter in which distinguishing our dust from the rest of the dust is at the extreme of remoteness, and which is the content of the report of our return, ﴿is a return﴾, i.e., a restoration to what we were upon, ﴿far-off [indeed]﴾, because it is not possible to distinguish our dust from the rest of the dust.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 50, verse 4:

Since the context is about the all-encompassing knowledge of what we know and what we do not know, the listener expects an answer concerning this ignorance. So He said, removing its cause and opening with the particle of expectation: ﴿Indeed﴾, meaning: rather, We are over that with complete power, because We ﴿have known﴾, by Our greatness, ﴿what the earth diminishes of them﴾, meaning: of their parts that are dispersed through their bodies after death and before it. For if a person were to grow by every food he eats and did not diminish, he would become like a mountain. Rather, We are constantly in the bringing into existence and the annihilation of those parts, and that is a branch of knowing each part at the time when its loss occurred, whether that part was small or large. None of that happens except by Our eyes (p. 406), by Our self-subsistence and by the penetrating knowledge of what is within as well as what is apparent, and by the preservation to which no incapacity, heedlessness, or anything else can be attributed.

However, He expressed it with ﴿min﴾ (of), because the earth does not consume the coccyx ('ajb al-dhanab), for it is like the seed for the bodies of the children of Adam.

Since it is the custom among all people that what is written is preserved, He applied the matter to what their customs have been accustomed to, so He said, indicating with the plural of majesty to His independence from the Book: ﴿And with Us is a Book﴾, meaning: according to what We possess of majesty, independent of everything, ﴿a Book﴾, meaning: comprehensive of everything, ﴿preserved﴾, meaning: thorough in preservation, from which nothing among things escapes, whether small or large. So how do they find it improbable, given Our greatness, that We would be unable to distinguish their dust from the dust of the earth [and nothing of a part of it has become mixed in Our knowledge with anything of another part, let alone that anything of it should mix with another thing of the dust of the earth] or of other things.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 50, verse 5:

Since the implied sense is: "They do not deny this of Our greatness, because they acknowledge that We created the heavens and the earth, and created them from dust, and that We send down water so that vegetation grows," He turned away from this to His saying: ﴿Nay, they have denied the truth⦆ — that is, the matter that is firmly established, than which nothing is more firmly established — ﴿when it came to them﴾ — that is, when it came to them — because what stirred within them, out of their amazement that a messenger should be sent to them from among themselves, was the portion of the souls' desires and the domination of their whims, out of envy on their part, without reflection on what they had said, nor consideration of it, nor pondering. Therefore they said what is unintelligible: that the One who is able to originate something from non-existence and bring it into being is not able to restore it after its annihilation and destruction.

Since their adherence to this feeble saying and their being bound by its obligation resulted in confusion in their opinion — whether they would return and be ascribed to ignorance, frivolity, foolishness and rashness, or would persist in it, which, together with their disbelief in the One who created them, would lead to something even greater than that: fighting and killing, and being ascribed to frivolity and ignorance — He expressed this meaning by saying: ﴿So they are﴾ — that is, because of their hastening to this worthless saying — ﴿in a confused matter﴾ — that is, very disturbed and mixed up, from *maraj*, which is the intermixing of vegetation with different kinds. Thus they [at times] say: "Magic," at other times "soothsaying," at other times "poetry," at other times "lies," and at other times something else. Disturbance necessarily entails disagreement, and that is the strongest proof of falsehood, just as firmness and sincerity necessarily entail agreement, and that is the strongest proof of truth. Al-Hasan said: "No people have abandoned the truth without their affair becoming confused," and Qatadah said likewise, adding: "and their religion became confused for them."

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 50, verse 6:

When He had informed them that they had said this without reflection, He rebuked them for it, denounced them, and indicated the correctness of what they denied and the corruption of their denial, by His saying, tracing it back to their haste toward falsehood: ﴿Have they not looked at the sky above them?﴾ That is, with the eye of sight and of insight, ﴿to the sky﴾, that is, the one that encompasses them and the earth on which they stand. Since this term is applied to everything that is high above, such as a ceiling or clouds and other things, even though it is most apparent in the starry ceiling, He clarified it by His saying: ﴿above them﴾, for others are only above some of them, not above all. Since its state is marvelous, it deserves to be asked about its manner, and so He indicated this with the interrogative particle, saying: ﴿How We have built it﴾, that is, how We brought it into existence, with the glory and might that are Ours, built like a tent, except that it is without pillars. ﴿And adorned it﴾, that is, with what is in it of small and large stars, both wandering and fixed. ﴿And there are no cracks in it﴾; that is, the state is that it has no ﴿cracks﴾, that is, openings, apertures, or fissures, but rather it is smooth, its parts closely joined. If this adornment is beneath it, then the One who set that in this firm arrangement which they witness, with its benefits and its covering that does not fail over the passage of the two renewals (night and day), possesses power by which nothing can overcome Him. If the adornment is above it, the same holds. If part of it is above and part below, the matter is still greater. This indicates that the sky is a sphere hollow in its middle, vaulted like an egg; for the negation of cracks in it, in this emphasized manner, indicates that clearly. He used the singular "sky" and did not pluralize it, because its being built as mentioned, though one, indicates perfect power; for a hollow structure cannot be completed by its builder without having openings, and if that were defective, the point of joining would be evident to onlookers, with whatever cracks, fissures, deficiencies and the like are in it, and he would not be able, with that, to leave it; if he were inside it, he would not be able to guard its exterior, and if he were outside it, he could not guard its interior. This world is preserved from its outside and its inside, so it is known that its Maker is exalted above being characterized by what the intellects encompass, by being within knowledge or outside it, connected to it or separate from [it], or needing a god in the making or a helper or assistant in the preservation. He used the plural "cracks" to indicate the intended sense of the genus with regard to the sky, after the singular form of the word had conveyed it; so the plural together with the intended genus indicates distribution, while conveying that the Builder, had He needed a single opening for this vast creation of wide sides and distant extents, would have needed many openings.

For this great body does not suffice with a single opening for one who needs movement. Thus He sent down the speech of the All-Knowing, the All-Aware, in accordance with such meanings. It should not be supposed that any artifice of craftsmanship was altered in it merely for the sake of the rhyme (fāṣila); for that happens only to one who is needy, and God is exalted above that. It is permissible, and it is the better view, that by "cracks" is meant the capacity for growth, like the earth, through which water permeates so that the roots of trees and plants extend within it and appear from it. It is also permissible that by it is meant "flaws", as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿You see in the creation of the Most Merciful no discrepancy. Return your gaze; do you see any rift?﴾ [al-Mulk: 3], that is, a defect, disagreement, or corruption; and this does not negate doors and ascents. And God knows best.

(p-410) When Allah, glory be to Him, had shown through the sign of the heaven His complete power, perfect knowledge, and the other attributes of perfection, He followed this with an indication that He cannot be described as being within the world or outside it, for He is neither joined to it nor separate from it. He drew attention to this by pointing to the sign of the earth, and placed it after the heaven, because the heaven is a stronger indication of the glory that this context is about: it is more wondrous in its making, higher in its elevation, greater in its rank, and more far-reaching in its effect. As for the earth, because of its constant nearness to people and their gathering of its fruits, a person heedlessly overlooks its indication, despite the crafts and benefits it contains. So He said: ﴿And the earth﴾, that is, the one surrounding them, ﴿We have spread it out﴾, that is, We made it, by virtue of Our greatness, spread out and not raised into a hump. Since what is spread out might tilt, He said: ﴿And We cast into it firm mountains﴾, that is, mountains that are fixed, which were the cause of its stability; and they differ from the custom of anchors in that they are from above, whereas anchors are set by you from below.

Since its inhabitants have an indispensable need for provision, He said, bestowing favor upon them: ﴿And We caused to grow in it﴾ by Our greatness ﴿of every beautiful pair﴾. He magnified its power by using partitive, saying: ﴿of every pair﴾, that is, every kind of plant whose kinds pair with one another, for all of your provisions, ﴿beautiful﴾, that is, it is at the utmost of freshness and delightfulness. Thus it was, along with being provision, a source of recreation.

When he mentioned these marvelous creations, he gave the reason for them with His saying: ﴿an insight﴾, meaning: We made all these things so that you would look at them with your eyes and then reflect with your insights, passing through them to their Maker and knowing the greatness that belongs to Him. ﴿And a reminder﴾, meaning: and so that you would be reminded by them with a great remembrance, through the powers and capacity you have, so that by your incapacity regarding each of those things you would know that its Maker is not overcome by anything, and that He encompasses all the attributes of perfection. Had any blemish of imperfection touched His sublime presence, this wondrous, marvelous creation would never have flowed forth from Him.

Since one who does not benefit from a thing is as if he lacks it, he restricted the matter to the one who benefits, saying: ﴿for every servant﴾ who remembers, through what he has of deficiency and through what this creation indicates of perfection, that he is a servant owned by his Creator. Since man, because of his deficiency, is always such that whenever his intellect raises him up, his nature brings him down, he may think he will not be accepted when he returns. So, out of desire for returning, He says: ﴿turning penitently﴾, meaning one who repeatedly turns back from what his nature has lowered him to, toward what his intellect raises him to. Thus he returns from witnessing these acts to witnessing these attributes, and from these attributes to knowledge of the Essence.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 50, verse 9:

When the sending down of water was the most manifest of the signs and the clearest proof that He (exalted is He) is far too great to be described as being inside the world or outside it, or joined to it or separated from it, while through it there comes about the growing of plants, the availability of sustenance, and the life of everything, He singled it out as a reminder of this, saying: ﴿And We send down﴾, i.e., gradually, at times, in a continuous flow, and in a manner befitting Our greatness, which cannot be matched, by an unseen means, with its transport, its gushing forth, and its penetrating force. Then it descended all at once, destroying what it fell upon, so that what was a benefit became a harm. ﴿from the sky﴾, i.e., from the lofty place in which water is not held back from continuous falling except by an overpowering One, ﴿blessed water﴾, i.e., extremely beneficial, established, not a passing illusion, encompassing (p-412) all of your benefits.

Since water is the cause of the existence of things, and since this is the cause of its solidifying until it becomes timber, grain and grapes, and other wonders, He said: ﴿So We caused to grow﴾, speaking in the plural of majesty, ﴿by it gardens﴾, of fruit, trees, crops and other things that gardens comprise, which cover - i.e., conceal - whoever enters them. And since the stalk that is harvested, whose grain is food for animals and whose straw is for livestock, He specified it by His saying: ﴿and grain of the harvest﴾, i.e., the produce that is typically reaped, such as wheat, barley and the like. By the restriction, He also indicates that these grains are nobler than the grain of pearls that God brings forth from the rain, because the former sustain the plant, while the latter are for adornment.

Since the date palm is among the most wondrous of the trees that grow from the earth, together with the many benefits it has which no other tree shares, and since it corresponds to crops in height and shortness, and in being a staple food for humans and animals, He said: ﴿And the date palms, towering⦆ — that is, lofty and tall above all fruit-bearing trees, possessing goodly fruits ﴿with spathes of fruit stacked⦆ — despite the dryness of their trunks. ﴿Spathes⦆ (ṭalʿ) means arranged and piled up, one layer above another. It is the inner part of its spathe (ḥashw ṭalʿihi). The ṭalʿ is that which emerges from the top of the palm, as if it were two closed sheaths, with the clustered fruit (ḥaml naḍīd) between them, and its tip is defined. Or the ṭalʿ is what appears of the palm's fruit at the first moment of its appearance, and that covering is called the kufrā, because it covers it more firmly and securely than anything else. The ṭalʿ resembles the thick milk (al-labā) that forms in the udder of a she-camel (al-nāqa) before parturition; then, after it unites in whiteness, the ṭalʿ separates, at the time of ripening (al-yunūʿ), into red, yellow, green and other strange colours and wondrous attributes. These encompass benefits: fruit for enjoyment in several kinds, food, and other uses. Its ṭalʿ differs from the usual habit of most trees, for their fruits are single, each berry separate from its sister.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 50, verse 11:

When He, glory be to Him, mentioned some of the greatness that belongs to Him in the water, He mentioned for it a cause that is the utmost in bounty upon creation, so He said: ﴿a provision for the servants﴾. That is: We caused that (vegetation) to grow by it, for the reason that it is part of what We made their provision.

Since that was the greatest reminder to those with insight of the Resurrection and of all the attributes of perfection, He followed it with what it contains of reminder of the Resurrection in particular, so He said: ﴿And We revived thereby﴾, that is, by the water, by Our greatness, ﴿a dead land﴾. He named it "land" (balda) with the feminine ta' as an indication that it is in the utmost weakness and need of being firm and of being empty of it (the water). He mentioned His saying ﴿dead﴾ to increase the affirmation of the firmness of the need within it. Since this is especially among the clearest proofs of the Resurrection, He said, as a conclusion: ﴿Thus will be the coming forth﴾, that is, a similar great bringing forth, the coming forth which, because of its greatness, is as if it were specific to this meaning, namely the raising of the dead from their graves as they were in the world. There is no difference between the emergence of plants after they have been crushed in the earth and become dust, as was the case among their yellow, white, red, green and blue (varieties), and so on, and between the bringing forth of what has been crumbled of the dead as they were in the world.

Abu Hayyan said: He, exalted is He, mentioned three things concerning the sky: the building, the adornment, and the absence of fissures; and three concerning the earth: the spreading out, the casting of firm mountains, and the causing of growth. He paired the spreading with the building, because spreading is placing down and building is raising up; and the casting of the firm mountains with the adornment by the stars, because each of them is fixed (in place), that is, on the surface of what it is in; and the growth that follows the splitting, with the absence of fissures, so there is no split in it. In what the growth is connected to, He alluded to what is harvested every year while its root remains, and what is sown every year or two years and harvested every year, and to what is mixed of two kinds: so some fruits are fruit and not staple food, while most crops are staple food, and the date is both fruit and staple food.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 50, verse 12:

When the matter reached a point where there is no concealment in it, and it became established that they knew this, and that what drove them to openly deny it was nothing but hastening to it out of the dominance of desire without reflecting on its outcome, it fell under the category of committing an error (luzum al-ghalat). The context was about denying the resurrection which the warner from among the warned people had brought, so it was as if it were said: the denial of these people is more astonishing; has this ever happened to anyone at all? Then Allah the Exalted said, consoling this noble Prophet, since calamity becomes easier when it is widespread, and clarifying the glory of the Qur'an and the glory of its verses, as a confirmation of the warning and a caution through it, not as advice: ﴿Denied﴾. He marked the verb with the feminine ta' to indicate their insignificance in comparison with this glory. Since these aforementioned confederates, by their strength and multitude, were as if they were the people of glory entirely, having filled its time and place, he dropped the preposition and said: ﴿before them﴾.

Since they had no fame by which they were known, he said: ﴿the people of Noah﴾. And he pointed (p-415) to the great consolation in that a warner from among them came to them. They were so strong in carrying out what they attempted and so numerous that the minds cannot contain all their attributes. They harmed their messenger, and their harm lasted for nearly ten centuries. Since the final end of their affair was that the two waters converged upon them, the water of the sky and the water of the earth which rose up toward them, and it drowned them, he followed their story with that of their own group, by saying that the water descended upon them and destroyed them, because of the antithesis between their two states, as an indication of the great power and of acting by choice. So he said: ﴿and the companions of the Rass﴾, i.e., the well in which they were overturned, so it swallowed them along with whatever surrounded it, and it took them away with everything they had, as their story is mentioned in the Furqan.

Since the sign of [the people of] Salih is among the greatest proofs of the power to resurrect, and since their destruction was suitable to the destruction of those before them, for the companions of the Rass it was by the earthquake which is [at] the beginning of the swallowing, and for the people of Noah it was because the earthquake resulted from the cry which the wind carried, the wind whose nature is to carry the clouds that carry the water, he followed them with them, and they were companions of a well but were not swallowed with it, so he said: ﴿and Thamud﴾.

The people of Hud (peace be upon him) and the Copts were both destroyed. The former were destroyed by the wind that the Cry of Thamud had also afflicted, and the latter by water that God split apart by means of wind when Moses struck it with his staff. Both peoples were renowned for the greatness of their kingdoms and the might of their rule. He put first the one that was stronger in body and wider in dominion, because their destruction was the clearest proof of [God's] power and closest in resemblance to the destruction of Thamud. So He said: ﴿And 'Ad﴾. Then he joined to it (p-416) the two groups closest in resemblance to the destruction of the people of Noah and the People of the Rass, so He said: ﴿and Pharaoh﴾, singling him out, because no other disbeliever shares the same manner of drowning, and singling him out implies others. What has preceded in other surahs, more than once, describes him as a dominant king who made his people feel foolish, so they obeyed him. Thus their disbelief is known from their obedience to him, and this fits what comes before and after it. Since the context concerns obstinacy and opposition, there was no call to mention the Lord of the Stakes (dhu al-Awtad). Since the destruction of the overturned cities (al-Mu'tafikat) resembled, in its nature, the destruction of all who came before, by sinking into the earth and being submerged in water after being overturned in the air, He followed them with those peoples, referring to them with a term shorter than naming their tribes or cities, since they were a number of cities. He expressed it by "brotherhood" rather than "people," because the context is about denying one who is from among them, and this is more consolingly apt. So He said: ﴿and the brothers of Lot﴾, meaning his in-laws, who, through intermarriage, became bound to him in a way that resembled brotherhood, through mutual support for their kings and subjects against those who opposed him personally and his uncle Abraham, peace be upon them both, as its explanation has passed in al-Baqarah. Despite this, they treated him with the very word-form of this plural, namely wrongdoing toward him and toward themselves and others.

When the tree was the usual place of cool air and refreshment, and its people had been punished with the opposite of that, He said: ﴿And the companions of the Thicket﴾, because they shared with them in punishment by fire. Those were punished with stones of sulfur falling from above, and these [with fire] falling from the darkness of the clouds. He referred to them in the singular, and the intended meaning is the thicket (ghaydah), indicating that (p-٤١٧) from the density of its intertwining it was like a single tree. Since Tubba' (Tubba'), although he was a mighty king among his people, was opposed by them despite that, and since his people had a fire [in their land] to which they brought their disputes, which would consume the wrongdoer, He concluded with them, saying: ﴿And the people of Tubba'﴾, even though he was a ruler who called them to God. So it should not be thought that denial is restricted to the strong against the weak; rather, it befalls whomever We will, strong or weak, and nothing escapes Our will.

Since there was nothing here requiring emphasis of the kind that was explained in "Sad," He said, dispensing with it: ﴿Each﴾, that is, of these groups, ﴿denied the messengers﴾, that is, all of them by denying their messenger, for all are equal in what necessitates faith, namely the manifestation of helplessness and the call to God. ﴿So there was justified﴾ [that is], so there resulted from their denial of them that it was established against them and became binding, ﴿My warning﴾ [Qaf 50:45], [that is], that which they used to deny when they were warned of it. So We hastened for them from it in this world what We had decreed against them from eternity, and We destroyed them with a general destruction, like the destruction of a single soul, in various ways, as is well known to whoever has concern with such examples. We followed it with what is in the barzakh, and deferred what is in the Resurrection until the Raising, by Our destroying them across their distant abodes, their far-separated eras, and their great numbers, showing that We have all-encompassing comprehensiveness. So be consoled by your brother messengers and take them as a model, and let your people be warned of what befell those who denied them, if they persist.

(p-٤١٨) When He, glorified is He, had mentioned the consolation through the denial of these confederate peoples after mentioning the denial of Quraysh, and the establishment of decisive proofs against what they denied and the falsehood of their denial, and concluded with the realization of the threat, of which the first signs had been witnessed in their destruction, the truthfulness of the messengers was established, and the power over everything He wills with this creation, through bringing into existence and annihilation, was established. He then denied them the denial and rebuked them for it, affirming the realization of the threat. He said, as a consequence of their denial after what was mentioned, that He had created all existence: ﴿Were We then worn out by the first creation?﴾ That is: has there come to Us, with all of Our greatness, fatigue (al-i'a', meaning incapacity) due to creation in any part of its bringing into being or its annihilation, ﴿the first﴾, that is, of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, when We began it by originating it from non-existence, and of whoever created man and all the rest of the animals anew, and then at every moment in the stages that are witnessed, in these customary gradations, after We had created their origin in that manner, something having no origin in life; and in their annihilation after creating them all at once, like these nations, or gradually, like others, so that they might suppose, because of incapacity with the first creation, which is more difficult in the course of customary events than the repetition, that We would be incapable of repeating it a second time. It is said: "he was wearied (ʿayiya) by the matter," when he was not guided to its matter or to the manner of its intent, or was incapable of it and could not accomplish its perfection.

Since the estimation was certain by what the interrogative hamza of denial (hamzat al-inkar, the hamza used to express rejection) indicates, the meaning is: We were not wearied by that, but We brought it into being with the utmost perfection for the container and the contained, and they know this and do not deny it, and they acknowledge the complete power over it; and within it is the acknowledgment of resurrection, though they are unaware of it. He turned away from it because of their statement, which undermines their belief in it, so He said: ﴿Rather, they are in confusion about a new creation.﴾ That is: in intense confusion and doubt, which necessitates speaking with a jumbled speech of which no meaning can be understood; rather, silence about it is more beautiful. ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "O neighbour, it is indeed confused for you; know the truth and you will know its people." Satan confused them by adorning for them the claim that resurrection is outside the customary course, so they abandoned for that reason the sound analogy (al-qiyas al-sahih, reasoning by analogy) and the judgment by the more evident path ﴿concerning﴾ a ﴿new creation﴾, that is, the repetition.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 50, verse 16:

When he mentioned the creation of the two horizons (al-khafiqayn), he followed it with the creation of that which comprises all that is in them, saying: ﴿And certainly﴾ that is, [and] the state is that We have indeed ﴿created﴾, by the majesty that belongs to Us, ﴿man (al-insan)﴾, who is more wondrous in creation and more comprehensive than all that has been mentioned before, with what is in him of intimacy and rebellion, remembrance and forgetfulness, ignorance and knowledge, obedience and disobedience, and other wondrous matters of affair. We have appointed over him from Our hosts one who guards him, keeping account of his movements and stillnesses and all of his states. ﴿And We know﴾, that is, and the state is that We know, by the comprehensiveness that belongs to Us, ﴿what his soul whispers (tuwaswisu)﴾, that is, speaks in a hidden manner,

﴿to him﴾ now and in what follows of that which has not yet sprung forth from the treasuries of the unseen into the secret (sirr) of the self, just as We know what he speaks. ﴿His soul (nafsuhu)﴾, which is the thoughts (al-khawatir) that present themselves to him, so that he himself perhaps is unable to control them. So We know that their hearts are aware of Our power to do what We will in the most perfect manner, and of the soundness of the Qur'an, its inimitability, and the truthfulness of the Messenger (ﷺ) in conveying it, and his distinction. Rather, envy, jealousy, arrogance (al-kibr) and leadership (al-ri'asa) led them to deny with their tongues, until that became a character trait for them, and they persisted in it until it covered over their intellects, so they came to be in a confusion encompassing them [from] all sides.

Since the one who knows a thing, the nearer he is to it, the more firm and certain his knowledge of it becomes, He said, giving an image of His knowledge and depicting it by that which we know necessitates it: ﴿And We are﴾ by the majesty that belongs to Us ﴿nearer to him﴾, nearness of knowledge and witnessing, without any distance, ﴿than the jugular vein (hablu al-warid)﴾, because its parts and components veil one another, whereas nothing veils the knowledge of God. What is meant by it is the category (al-jins), and the two veins (al-waridan) are two vessels like two cords, flanking the two sides of the neck at its front, connected from the head to the aorta (al-watin), which is the vessel of the heart. This is a metaphor for extreme nearness. Its annexation is like "masjid al-jami'". What is useful here was already mentioned in the commentary on Surah al-Ma'idah at His saying: ﴿And Allah will protect you from the people﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 67]. Al-Qushayri said: In this verse there is awe, fear and dread for one group, and spirit, intimacy and tranquility of heart for another group.

Since He, glory be to Him, has appointed over us guardians who preserve our deeds and record our words and states, and it is known to us that the reason for such safeguarding is fear of heedlessness and forgetfulness, He, glory be to Him, first announced the perfection of His knowledge, so that this feared danger was removed. He attached it to the nearest thing, or we know (p-421) His saying, as an emphasis on what is known of the comprehensiveness of His knowledge and of His not needing [the guardians], and as a warning by means of what is nearer to our familiar experience: ﴿When﴾, that is, at the time when ﴿there receive﴾, that is, with the utmost diligence, vigilance and attentiveness, ﴿from every person whom We created and brought into this existence﴾ ﴿the two receivers﴾. And what will make you know what they are? They are two great angels, ﴿seated on the right﴾ of every person ([one of them seated]) ﴿and on the left﴾, likewise, ﴿seated﴾, that is, stationed and confined to positions for that person with the most thorough placement. ﴿And We are nearer to him than they are﴾ and better aware. We appointed them as guardians only to establish proof through them regarding the patterns of your conduct and other wisdoms.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 50, verse 18:

When the acts of the tongue, the heart, and the body arise from the speech of the soul (kalam al-nafs, the inner speech), and speech is comprehensive, He said, explaining the all-encompassing nature of His knowledge by the all-encompassing nature of the One who appointed (the two angels) to guard this comprehensive creation, in answer to one who seems to have asked: what do the two receivers (al-mutalaqqiyan) do? ﴿Not a word does he utter﴾, i.e., the accountable person casts forth and emits from his mouth, and he generalized in the negation by His saying ﴿but there is with him﴾, i.e., with the human or the word, in a state of power and majesty that is among the most wondrous of wonders, ﴿a watcher﴾ from Our guardians, most attentive to him in each of his conditions, ﴿ready﴾, i.e., present, watching, not heedless in any way. Al-Baghawi narrated with his chain, through the route of al-Tha'labi, from Abu Umamah (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The recorder of good deeds is on the right of the man, and the recorder of bad deeds is on the left of the man, and the recorder of good deeds is superior to the recorder of bad deeds. When he does a good deed, the one on the right records it as ten; and when he does a bad deed, the one on the right says to the one on the left: 'Leave him for seven hours, perhaps he will glorify (Allah) or seek forgiveness.'"

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 50, verse 19:

Since the likeness of the sending forth of the two horizons (al-khafiqayn), then death, then the blast (al-nafkh), is by the sending of the King into the world to the people for their presentation (al-'ard), a person among them becomes one who strives to adorn himself for the King with what pleases Him, toward the purpose of that presentation, within the term He has set for them. When that time comes, which is like death, the messengers seize him and bring him, and whoever they have brought among them they detain at the door of the King until those being presented are complete. When their gathering is complete and they are ordered to stand for the presentation, the herald (al-munadi) shouts to them with the trumpet called al-nafir, which is like the Trumpet (al-sur). Therefore the Exalted said, explaining the encompassing of His power over all His creation, connecting it to what is implied by the context: ﴿And the man who is charged with it will be agitated at the appointed time, in which he is ordered to move about, with what pleases God in word and deed, according to His will, glorified is He, whether it is in conformity with the command or in opposition to it,﴾ until the time of departure arrives, expressed in the past tense as an alert that death, although it is inevitable, is very near: ﴿And the agony of death has come﴾, i.e., came and arrived, ﴿[the] agony of death﴾, i.e., its state at the time of extraction, its severity and its overwhelming, by which the dying person becomes like one intoxicated, not comprehending, and his states, actions and words depart from the law of moderation. And it comes ﴿with the truth﴾ (bil-haqq), i.e., the fixed matter to which reality corresponds, so there is no stratagem to guard against it, from the failure of the senses and the removal of the veil concerning the conditions of the barzakh, from the trial of questioning and constriction of the space or its expansiveness. It is said to the dying person, by the tongue of his state if not by the tongue of speech: ﴿That﴾, i.e., this great matter, lofty in rank, which every person deserves to prepare for with utmost seriousness, ﴿is what you were﴾ (kunta) by nature and disposition. Since his aversion from it and his flight from its occurrence, by preserving health and seeking the remedy of delay, were at their utmost, it was as though he fled from nothing but it. He indicated this by placing the prepositional phrase first, so He said: ﴿from it you would shrink﴾, i.e., you would incline away, recoil, be alarmed, and flee.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 50, verse 20:

Since the sense is: that person is seized by force from among family, brothers, kinsfolk and neighbours, and is joined to the host of the dead, who are in the barzakh (the intermediate state) as those who have alighted, and as those who have settled to await the rest of them, and they remain so until those who are coming to them are complete and have reached them, he follows it with his saying, explaining the encompassing of the world of the malakut (dominion), the might and the jabarut (majesty): ﴿And the Trumpet will be blown﴾, i.e., by the slightest gesture and the easiest command, ﴿into the Trumpet﴾, which is the horn into which Israfil, peace be upon him, will blow for the general death and the general resurrection when completion is reached and the time of dealings is cut off. Its greatness and vastness are such that none knows its extent except Allah, exalted is He. He, peace be upon him, has been holding the Trumpet to his mouth since the Prophet ﷺ was sent, bowing his forehead and inclining his hearing, waiting for when he will be commanded. How great a magnitude it is, and how heedless we are of it, and how it has made us forget it, and how we have felt secure from it! The intended meaning of this is the blast of resurrection.

Since that effect from the self is the secret of existence, and he pointed to its greatness by his saying: ﴿That﴾, i.e., the great time, abounding in terrors, quakings and frights, ﴿is the Day of the Promised Threat﴾, i.e., the day in which what was threatened will occur.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 50, verse 21:

Since the implied sense is: from that blast there came a terrifying cry and an all-encompassing tremor, so people rose en masse from their graves, and what was in their breasts was brought out, he followed it with his words, as an explanation of the all-inclusiveness of the gathering (al-'ard): ﴿And every soul will come, with it a driver and a witness.﴾ That is, every soul that is responsible [being] ﴿with it a driver﴾ who drives it toward that which it deeply dislikes, because of his knowledge of the shortcomings it had committed ﴿and a witness﴾ who testifies against it concerning what it did. The apparent meaning here is that the driver has no connection whatsoever to the testimony, lest that soul say that he is an adversary, and an adversary's testimony is not accepted. Then, in an emphatic style, it is said at that time to the one who neglected deeds, following what he deserved to deny in the world, and as an alert that its magnitude makes it something that rightly calls for emphasis:

﴿Indeed you were﴾ meaning: in a state that became as though it were your natural disposition, ﴿in heedlessness﴾ meaning: a great heedlessness that enveloped you and arose within you, ﴿from this﴾ meaning: from conceiving of this Day as it truly is, with the severing of all means and the recompense of reward or punishment. For despite its extreme clarity, it is hidden from those who follow their desires. ﴿So We removed﴾ by Our greatness, through death and then through resurrection, ﴿from you your covering﴾ which had been veiling you from seeing it, the heedlessness caused by hopes in status, wealth, and all other shares and desires. This confirms the encompassing knowledge of His, glory be to Him, in decree and in rendering powerless. From al-Wasiti: whoever has the covering of heedlessness lifted from him sees all things within the grip of power, and the realities of all things are disclosed to him in their entirety. This is an expression for knowledge of the states of the Resurrection.

Since this unveiling resulted in complete disclosure, He expressed it with His words: ﴿So your sight today﴾ meaning: after the resurrection, ﴿is sharp﴾ meaning: in the utmost keenness and penetration. Therefore you will acknowledge what you used to deny.

When Allah, may He be exalted, informed of what the angels, or whoever He wills of His hosts, would say to him, and He had already informed that the objects of their worship, from idols, devils and others, would become adversaries to them on the Day of Resurrection, He then informed of what the companion (al-qarin) would say, from the driver, the witness, and the devil whose discourse was mentioned earlier in Surat al-Zukhruf. So He said, [coordinating] with the statement implied before "laqad" (indeed), expressing it in the past tense for emphasis on its content and affirmation: ﴿And his companion will say﴾, that is, the devil who was empowered to mislead him and lure him toward what he desires. Al-Kirmani transmitted this from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both.

﴿This is﴾, that is, the human being whom You paired me with. Since the matter in each of the obedient and the disobedient is extremely strange, because the obedient one opposes his own desire, so he becomes an angel-like being, stripped of his portions and the impulses of his soul and of what it is built upon of deficiencies and appetites, while the disobedient one is at the disposal (yad) of the devil, who directs him toward his aims however he wills, so he obeys him with utmost appetite while knowing his enmity, and that obedience to him cannot occur except by opposing the command of Allah, the Protector, the Loving. And the disobedient ones are so numerous that the obedient ones among them are, in comparison, like a white hair on the hide of a black bull. Since this was contrary to reason, He indicated this opposition by the particle used for one who does not understand, and indicated all the strangeness in His command by "ladayya" (with me), so He said: ﴿What is with me﴾, that is, [the matter] which is with me of the extremely strange affair, since the one who obeys has disobeyed me. He is naturally disposed to the deficiencies and portions which he sees as his life, pleasure and comfort, while the disobedient one has obeyed me, though he knows by his reason that I am pure evil, and has abandoned pure good while knowing that this leads to his ruin. ﴿Ready﴾, that is, present and prepared for what is required of him.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 50, verse 24:

Since it is the custom that whoever is presented with something hastens to carry out its command by word or deed, he joined to that what is its result, and he began with the rebellious one, because the context concerns him. So he said what indicates that he has no weight, so there is no pause in his punishment, neither at his reckoning nor otherwise, emphasizing it by addressing the one who is to be emphasized by the casting, or by addressing the driver and the witness, or the driver alone, making the pronoun dual for the command, as if he said: "Cast, cast," for emphasis and to inspire awe: ﴿Cast both﴾, that is, throw down, pushing him without compassion. It was said: rather, it is a dual form. The origin of this is that the minimum company is three, so the speech of one went according to his companion. Do you not see that poets most often say: "O my two companions" (yā ṣāḥibayya), "O my two friends" (yā khalīlayya)? The secret in it, when the addressee is one, is conveying that the act is demanded from him with great earnestness, his strength in it being equal to the strength of two. ﴿Into Hell﴾, that is, the fire in which the one cast is met with what he used to do to God's servants: arrogance, scowling, aversion, and fanaticism.

Since the aim was to give the reason for his casting by a description that covers others as well, so that it would be a kindness to whoever God wills to protect among those who hear this speech, and a proof against whoever God wills to humiliate: ﴿every obstinate disbeliever﴾, that is, one who excessively conceals the truth and is hostile to its people without any proof, out of zealotry and arrogance, viewing what is with him as good and persisting in it with tyranny and pride over what others have, disdaining them, whoever he may be. (p-427)

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 50, verse 25:

﴿Mannaʿin﴾ means: one who greatly withholds ﴿lil-khayr﴾ (from good), of wealth and otherwise, and from every act of kindness connected with wealth, speech, or deeds. ﴿Muʿtadin﴾ means: one who transgresses the limits. ﴿Murib﴾ means: one who falls into doubt (rayb), which is suspicion and accusation in matters of religion, and who causes others to fall into it. Then he made ﴿kull﴾ (every) the subject of the following phrase as an explanation (badal/bayan) of his excessive disbelief, which made every evil obligatory for him.

﴿Who set up﴾ a doubled disbelief, obstinacy, and withholding of the good that is obligatory for him in his heart, tongue, and body, and a transgression of bounds by entering into doubt and drawing others into it. ﴿Alongside God﴾, i.e., the One who encompasses all attributes of perfection, so His affair is not hidden from any person of intellect, ﴿a god﴾.

Since a stubborn person might twist the verse and apply it to one who calls upon God by a name other than this greatest Name, he stated the intended meaning explicitly with His words: ﴿another﴾. The word also implies that it is derived from "ta'akhkhur" (lateness), which looks to baseness and to falling out of consideration entirely from [ʿayn] regard.

Since this person denied the truth that is owed to God for His essence, setting aside everything else, and then what is owed to Him because of His lordship and His bestowal of favor on every existent, and then because of His continuing kindness despite disobedience, through forbearance, and since he was obstinate in this and in ascribing to another what cannot be valid for it in any respect, the verse explained his description by saying: ﴿Throw him into the punishment﴾, i.e., the [ayy] punishment that removes [kull] all sweetness, ﴿the severe﴾.

Since the companion had said what has preceded, intending by it—out of his ignorance—to escape the punishment by showing that he himself does not possess the attributes of this self but is rather among the great believers, his speech was answered by the casting of that self. The reason given for the command to cast it was that it encompasses this companion too. So the listener eagerly awaits what will become of his state. It is the custom that whoever speaks about a person of the same faults—especially if he was the cause of them, or that person had spoken about him—then by analogy it necessarily follows that that self will say something about itself. This is at the time of the command to cast it: "Our Lord, he made me transgress." God answered at this point of eager anticipation, saying: ﴿His companion said﴾, calling out with the omission of the particle of address, the way of those close to Him, giving the impression that he is one of them: ﴿"Our Lord﴾, O You who bestow goodness [upon us], O all creatures: ﴿"I did not make him transgress﴾, that is, I did not bring him into what he was in of transgression, for I have no authority over him, and You know that. ﴿"But he was﴾ by his innate nature and disposition (p-429) ﴿in far error﴾, encompassing him from all its sides, such that his return with it is impossible. For this reason he would hasten to everything that angers God, and if his drive toward it is missed, he needs not the slightest prompting, and so he flares up with the flare of one who is innately and firmly fixed in his temperament.

Since it was as if it were said: "With what is this answered, and will anything be accepted from him?" It is said: "No." ﴿He said﴾, that is, the King, Who encompasses everything in knowledge and power, Who decreed upon them from eternity: ﴿Do not dispute﴾, that is, do not begin disputation with this zeal and striving ﴿in My presence﴾, that is, in the abode of recompense, in this Presence which is far beyond what you used to perceive of reports about it, and more wondrous than what can be perceived with true perception. The unveiling of what the elite, nay, the elite of the elite, used to find strange has been completed, so the benefit of a new faith has passed by means of its unveiling. ﴿And indeed﴾, that is, while the situation is that ﴿I had already sent forward﴾, that is, I had advanced, that is, I had commanded and admonished before this time, conveying and warning ﴿to you﴾, that is, everything that ought to be sent forward, so that no ambiguity remained and I left no one a proof in any respect, and I made that, out of kindness toward you, accompanied ﴿by the warning﴾, that is, the threat, which is the great terror upon all that you committed of disbelief and transgression, at the time when this Presence was [the] unseen of the unseen, veiled by veils of majesty and greatness, and rather, what lay below it of the unseen was hidden. Thus faith in it was beneficial.

Since all times are present before Him, glorified is He, He expressed the reason for this with "mā" (which is for the present) rather than "lā" (which is for the future), so He said: ﴿What is changed﴾, i.e., what is altered from being altered, [that which was] in any way such that a substitute is made for it, so that there would be a change in it: ﴿the word is not changed in My presence﴾, i.e., the word that reaches you from My presence, whose strangeness cannot be encompassed, namely that whoever associates others with Me, I will not forgive him, and I forgive what is less than that for whomever I will. Pardoning some of the sinners is not a change, because the indications of pardon point to the restriction of the threat, and that it is conditioned by conditions. ﴿And I am not﴾, and He emphasized the negation, so He said: ﴿unjust to the servants﴾, i.e., not one who does injustice to the servants, neither to the companion (qarīn) nor to whoever led him astray nor to others, so that I would punish one who does not deserve it, or pardon one of whom I have said: "I will not forgive him," and I have commanded My hosts, and they opposed him on My account. Had I pardoned him, I would have been, along with changing the word, having wronged them by honoring those who opposed him on My account, and nothing more.

The commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 50, verse 30:

Since this statement is of such terrifying import and its mention uproots hearts, he depicted its time in a form that increases that terror. Speech falls short of describing it, and no one can hope to be delivered from it by strength or power. So he said, meaning: [this] all [occurs] ﴿on the day﴾. Since the purpose was to inform that Hell is vast despite its narrowness, so that it can contain countless creatures, and that, despite its aversion to those who burn in it and its scowling at them, it loves their rushing into it and their being brought to it, he expressed this by way of kināya (metonymy) with the words ﴿We will say﴾, meaning, by the greatness we possess, which nothing may be hidden from, ﴿to Hell﴾, the abode of punishment, with its aversion, sternness and scowling, to manifest the terror through depicting the matter with which it is threatened, to rebuke the disbelievers, and to alert whoever hears this report to beware of heedlessness about this question: ﴿Are you filled?﴾. So Our word is fulfilled: ﴿I will surely fill Hell with jinn and men all together﴾ [Hud: 119]. This will be after creatures have been cast into it in numbers that description cannot encompass, and then it will say: No.

﴿And it will say﴾, in obedience to God, out of love for the torment of His enemies, and to inform that it has not been filled, because it is in the nature of Hell that whenever more fuel is added to it, its flame increases: ﴿Is there any more?﴾, meaning: any increase, or any of the disobedient as an addition, whether many or few; for I receive whatever is brought to me, and it will remain so, as has been related in the hadith: ««Hell will not cease to have [people] cast into it, and it will say: Is there any more? until the Mighty One places His foot in it»». That is, He strikes it with the whip of humiliation out of His majesty, so that parts of it draw together into one another, and it says: Qat, qat (enough, enough), by Your might. Then they [the people] will remain between the extremes of heat and the zamharir (bitter cold). God, glory be to Him, has made a sign of this in this abode through the alternation of time between heat and cold: when heat becomes excessive, His mercy brings cold and water from the sky, and they mix together so that there is moderation; and when cold becomes excessive, His mercy brings heat through the sun, and the two existences mix, so there is moderation for Him. All of that is governed by circuits measured in equitable proportions, known by the decree of the Mighty, the All-Knowing. Ibn Burjan mentioned this.

(p-431)

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 50, verse 31:

When He mentioned the Fire and placed it first, because the context is one of warning, He followed it with the Abode of the Righteous (dar al-abrar). Giving them good news, with the removal of the burden of travel and the folding up of the distance, He said: ﴿And Paradise will be brought near to the God-fearing﴾, i.e., brought close, with the easiest of matters, together with the ranks (darajat) and the full basins (hiyad, sing. hawd), ﴿Paradise brought near for the God-fearing﴾, i.e., those who are foremost (al-'arikin) in this description. So when they see it, they race toward it and leave behind what they were in of the (p-432) station of standing, [such as] the pulpits of light, the dunes of musk, and the like. As for others among the people of faith, they may have a different description, so that those who feared God are driven to it, as has passed in Surat al-Zumar.

And since nearness is a relative matter, He emphasized it with His saying: ﴿not far off﴾, i.e., a bringing near such that it cannot be described as distant.

This is the nazm-based commentary of al-Biqa'i on Surah Qaf (50) verse 32, and the passage ends mid-argument, so I translate it as it stands.

When bringing near (al-taqrib) may not be understood by the beholder in its cause, He said, addressing them with good news: ﴿This is﴾, that is, the bringing near and what you see of everything that gladdens you, ﴿what﴾, that is, the matter ﴿that you were promised﴾, that is, the promise to you concerning it was made in the world. He expressed it with the present tense (al-mudari') to relate the past state as if it were present, and He expressed the bringing near with the past tense (al-madi) to confirm its matter and to depict its presence now, so that the present tense used for the promise would be in its most firm position. He left the matter indefinite, because that is more stirring of desire, and specification after indefiniteness is more delightful. Therefore He said, explaining for the God-fearing (al-muttaqin), repeating the preposition (li) because of what came between it and the substituted noun of the parenthetical clause, as an answer to one who seems to have asked: "For whom is this promise?" Then Exalted is He said: ﴿for every one who turns back (awwab)﴾, that is, one who returns to uprightness through the piety of the heart if some crookedness appears in his outward conduct, and by this He draws attention to the fact that, out of His bounty, He did not make the continuance of uprightness a condition for the validity of describing him with piety, ﴿who keeps watch (hafiz)﴾, that is, one who is emphatic in guarding the limits and all the covenants by persistence in uprightness and returning after a slip. Then He substituted from "every" [as a completion] for the explanation of the God-fearing the phrase:

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 50, verse 33:

﴿Whoever feared﴾ [the Most Merciful] without repeating the preposition, because there is no interruption before it as there was in the first case. He drew attention to the abundance of his fear by saying ﴿the Most Merciful﴾, because whoever fears while keeping in mind the all-encompassing mercy toward both the obedient and the disobedient, his fear, while keeping in mind other than that, is more fitting. Al-Qushayri said: The expression with this name is an indication that it is a fear accompanied by intimacy, meaning hope, as is prescribed. He said: For this reason He did not say "the Compeller" or "the Subduer." He said: It is said that khashya (awe-fear) is more subtle than khawf (fear); so it is close to hayba (reverential dread). ﴿In the unseen﴾, that is, accompanied by Him without seeking a sign or a matter by which he would reach the level of unveiling (mukashafa), but rather he is content with the decisive proofs, among which is that He is the One who nurtures and sustains, so he must have a Lord. This is also a statement of the complete extent of his fear.

Since the beneficial form of obedience is that which is constant until death, He said: ﴿And came﴾, that is, after death, ﴿with a heart turned in repentance﴾, that is, returning to God Most High through the restraint of knowledge. The word "soul" was not used, out of gentleness toward the sinners; for even if their souls fell short, they did not have the truthfulness of steadfast footing, so for them there is regret with their hearts and sincerity of remorse.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 50, verse 34:

Since the announcement that Paradise belongs to them, though a joyful matter, does not necessarily require their entering it at that very time, their joy was increased by the permission, expressed in His words, using the plural pronoun to clarify that what is meant by "man" (whoever) is all of the God-fearing: ﴿Enter it﴾, i.e., it is said to them: enter Paradise. Since the intent was to receive them with delight through the glad tidings, He said: ﴿in peace﴾, i.e., accompanied by safety from everything that could possibly be feared. Thus this led to His words, bringing the joy to a limit that cannot be described: ﴿That﴾, i.e., the very great day, ﴿is the day﴾ — a beginning or a confirmation — ﴿of eternity﴾, i.e., the abode that has no end, and none of its pleasures ever ceases at all. For this reason He connected to it His words, as an answer to one who seems to ask: in what manner is their eternity?

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 50, verse 35:

﴿For them﴾ in their outward and inward states ﴿is whatever they will﴾, that is: their will is renewed or enabled [for it] ﴿therein﴾, that is, in Paradise, ﴿and with Us﴾, that is, in Our presence, from matters that are of the utmost strangeness to them, even though everything they have is already marvelous ﴿is more﴾, that is: of what does not fall within their imaginings to will; for the context of divine favour indicates that its indefiniteness (tanwin) is for magnification, and the expression "with Us" (ladā) emphasises this in a manner befitting it, so that they are at every moment in an increase beyond their hopes, the reverse of what they were in the world. Thereby their knowledge increases, for the things that are within God's power are not confined, because His knowledge does not end.

When He, glory be to Him, mentioned at the beginning of the surah their denial of the power (of resurrection), while they acknowledged what would refute that denial, and then consoled (the Prophet) and warned with the denial of the earlier nations, mentioning His power over them, He followed this with evidence of the perfection of His power. He concluded with an indication that His power has no end, cannot be confined by any limit, and cannot be counted by any number. This was a refutation of the obstinate and of the innovators of ittihad (the heresy of unity of existence), who say: "What is possible is no more wondrous than what has occurred." He connected, after ﴿فَحَقَّ وعِيدِ﴾ [Q. 50:14], which I have supposed to be [the sense of] "then has the warning been fulfilled" concerning the destruction of those nations, something more general than it, in that it encompasses all of past time and is more indicative of the comprehensiveness of power. So He said: ﴿وكَمْ أهْلَكْنا﴾ ("And how many We destroyed"), meaning: by what We possess of greatness.

Since the intended meaning is the generalization of destruction across all times and to all nations, He removed the preposition, to show the comprehensiveness of power, and said: ﴿قَبْلَهُمْ﴾ ("before them"). He increased the indication of generality by affirming it in His saying: ﴿مِن قَرْنٍ﴾ ("of a generation"), meaning: a generation that was at the utmost of strength. He increased the explanation of strength by saying: (p-435) ﴿هُمْ﴾ ("they"), meaning: those generations, in their outward and inward states, ﴿أشَدُّ مِنهُمْ﴾ ("were mightier than them"), meaning: than the Quraysh, ﴿بَطْشًا﴾ ("in strength"), meaning: in power and in seizing what they wanted by violence, force and severity. The omission of the preposition here indicates that every one who was before the Quraysh was mightier than them.
