Its affirmation in Surah Ṣād indicates that those mentioned there as destroyed, together with the characteristic of the call mentioned there, were some of the destroyed and not all of them.

When He, glory be to Him, informed of their greater might, He made the following consequent: ﴿فَنَقَّبُوا﴾ ("so they ranged"), meaning: they made penetrations ﴿فِي البِلادِ﴾ ("through the lands"), by opening in them doors both physical and figurative, and by breaking through their extremities what no others were able to, and by going to great lengths in traveling through the nuqab (mountain passes), which are the paths of mountains and narrow roads, let alone wide ones and those in the plains, with their expansive minds, their penetrating opinions and their strong natures. Along with that, they searched for news and informed others of what had not reached them. Each of them was a nuqab in this, that is, a sign in it, so that through it they gained praiseworthy deeds or glories.

Since the sense is: "Yet they were not spared, despite their great ranging and its severity, from Our destruction by the calamities of time and the disasters of events," the question of every hearer was directed at what there is in that of wonders, severity, terror and fears, as a question of alerting the heedless and forgetful, and as a rebuke and reproach to the obstinate ignorant, by His saying: ﴿هَلْ مِن مَحِيصٍ﴾ ("Is there any escape?"), meaning: any way of deviation, any place of evasion, any refuge, however slight, from Our decree, so that these people might have any way to avert Our command.

(p. 436) When we have mentioned here admonitions that would make even inanimate matter dance, how much more so for one who claims to be among the leading critics, he produced his statement, emphasized because of the denial of the denier and the obstinacy of the obstinate: ﴿Indeed, in that﴾, i.e., in the [matter] wondrous of admonitions which we have varied here, in the wondrous methods and strange ways of destruction and other things as you see, ﴿is a reminder﴾, i.e., a very great reminder. Since one who takes heed through the fates of the destroyed may do so by being present and seeing their fate at the moment they are struck, or by seeing their traces afterwards, and sometimes by being told about them, he began with the one who sees, because he is more worthy of admonition and closer to remembrance, saying: ﴿for whoever has﴾, i.e., a great having, ﴿a heart﴾, which is at the utmost of greatness and luminosity. If he sees any of that, he is such that he understands what he sees and is strengthened by it. Whoever is not like that has no heart, because his heart, being not beneficial, is as nothing.

Since he had begun with the beholder, because he is more deserving of consideration and closer to recollection, he followed with the one to whom reports are conveyed, saying: ﴿or gives ear﴾, i.e., giving ear greatly, with the utmost attentiveness, until it is as if he throws something heavy from a height to a depth, ﴿the hearing﴾, i.e., the complete hearing, which has stripped itself of preoccupations, of worldly portions and other things, when it hears what is absent from it, ﴿while he﴾, i.e., [and] the state being that, in the state of giving ear, ﴿is a witness﴾, i.e., present wholly. So he is at the utmost of focusing thought and gathering the mind, and nothing of what is recited to him and conveyed to him escapes him. He is reminded by what we have reminded him of, from our power, through particulars, of what it produced of power over every thing. He saw the glory of the Qur'an, so he knew that it is the speech of God, heard it from Him, confirmed the Messenger, and accepted everything he reports. Whoever hears something but does not bring his mind to it is absent.

The first is the knower in potency (al-'ālim bi'l-quwwa), who is the one naturally disposed to complete readiness, such that he needs nothing but reflection, because of the perfection prepared in him for understanding what the Qur'an reminds of. The second is the deficient one, with the thickness of nature in him, such that he needs instruction, and is reminded on condition that he accepts wholly and removes all obstacles. Therefore the placement of the dividing ﴿or﴾ (أوْ المُقَسِّمَةِ) is very fitting. And it is known from this the great nobility of the Qur'an, in that it gives glad tidings to the complete and the deficient alike, and there is no obstacle to it except aversion.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 50, verse 38:

When He had shown the completeness of His knowledge and the all-encompassing reach of His power through the creation of man, following what He had mentioned of all the cosmic existences, and then through His annihilation of the various kinds of mankind in every age, He reminded (them) of the creation of something greater than man in magnitude, though man is a part of it, in another manner. So He said, connecting it to: ﴿And We certainly created man﴾ [Qaf: 16]. He emphasised it as an alert and a rebuke for those who deny the Resurrection, and He opened it with the particle of expectation (harf al-tawaqqu'), because whoever is reminded of the creation of one thing expects to be told about what is greater than it: ﴿And We certainly created﴾, that is, by the majesty that We possess, whose extent cannot be measured and whose limits cannot be encompassed, ﴿the heavens and the earth﴾ in the state they are in of vastness and abundance of benefits, ﴿and what is between them﴾ of matters without which the affair cannot be ordered according to the principle of causes and effects, ﴿in six days﴾: the earth in two days, its benefits in two days, and the heavens in two days. Had He willed, that would have been in less than the twinkling of an eye, but He ordained for us to be deliberate in that. ﴿And no weariness touched Us﴾ because of the majesty that We have, (p-438) ﴿of weariness﴾, that is, fatigue. For had it been so, it would have implied weakness, and weakness implies corruption, and something of that would have come about contrary to what We intended, so Our disposal of it would have differed from Our disposal of the rest. Yet you witness the matter in all of it on an equal footing, in the full execution of the command and the complete disposal. (From al-laghab, which is fatigue, and al-rish al-lughab, which is the corrupt.)

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 50, verse 39:

When Allah, glorified is He, had shown the comprehensiveness of (His) knowledge and the all-encompassing nature of (His) power, and had disclosed the matter in both respects with the utmost disclosure, the knowledge of the Beloved, the Powerful, of what the enemy does became a greater warning to the enemy and a greater good tiding to the friend (walī). On account of that, He caused to follow it His saying: ﴿So be patient over what﴾, that is, over all that ﴿they say﴾, that is, the disbelievers and others. [And since] their sayings are not befitting to the Most Holy Presence, He, glorified is He, commanded what indicates that this (saying) is by His will, and that it necessitates His transcendence and perfection; because He has subdued the one who says it to his saying. Had the matter been by the will of that speaker independently, it would have been at the utmost remove from Him, since it necessitates destruction. So He said: ﴿And glorify﴾, that is, perform the declaration of transcendence above every trace of deficiency, being clothed ﴿with the praise of your Lord﴾, that is, with the affirmation of the encompassing of all attributes of perfection for the Master who manages and who is good to you, by all these proofs with which He has singled you out, preferring you over all creation in all that ﴿before the rising of the sun﴾, by the dawn prayer (Ṣalāt al-Ṣubḥ), and what is fitting for Him of glorification other than it, ﴿and before the setting﴾, by the afternoon prayer (Ṣalāt al-ʿAṣr) and the noon prayer (Ṣalāt al-Ẓuhr) likewise. So the afternoon prayer is the foundation (aṣl) for that time, and the noon prayer is a follower (tabaʿ) of it.

When he mentioned what is more indicative of love for the One worshipped, because it is the time of dispersal [of the people] to the necessities on which their sustenance depends, and of returning for the purpose of bodily rest through eating, drinking, play and gathering together after dispersal and reunion, along with the clear indication in both times of the folding [of creation] and then its spreading out (p. 439), He followed it with what occurs at the time of stillness, meaning rest through the pleasure of lying down and sleep. So He said: ﴿And of the night﴾, that is, during some of its portions, ﴿glorify Him﴾ with the two prayers of Maghrib and 'Isha' and with the night prayer (qiyam al-layl), because the night is the time of seclusion, and seclusion is the most delightful form of intimate conversation.

When He mentioned the obligatory acts (fara'id), which cannot be avoided, in a manner that also encompasses the voluntary acts (nawafil) of prayer and other things, He followed them with the voluntary acts tied to them. So He said: ﴿and after the prostrations﴾, that is, the most complete part of them, which is the obligatory prayer together with the regular sunnah prayers offered after it (rawatib), and glorification by speech as well. Al-Razi said: "Know that the reward of the words depends on the capacity for their issuing from hearts filled with knowledge and wisdom, and that the heart's eye should turn as the tongue turns, observing their realities and meanings. So glorification (tasbih) is the declaration of transcendence above everything that can be imagined by the mind, or formed in the imagination, or impressed upon the senses, or revolve in the thoughts, and praise (hamd) reveals the favour, the act of creating, and that He alone is the sole Giver of blessings." End of quotation.

Its meaning is that this praise is the reality; when it settles in the hearts, it stands upon the tongue and takes form in the limbs. It is understood as referring to the prayer, because it is the best of acts of worship, and it combines, through its words and actions, the two aspects of remembrance: transcendence (tanzih) and praise (tahmid). These two prayers which are mentioned first are the best of prayers, so they are the greatest instances in which glorification occurs together with praise (p. 440). The meaning, and God knows best, is that turning to Him is a seeking of rain from the One praised and glorified for victory over the deniers, and that prayer is the greatest remedy for victory and for the removal of distress. For this reason, "when a matter troubled the Prophet ﷺ, he would turn to prayer."

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 50, verse 41:

When Allah, glory be to Him, had consoled him (ﷺ) regarding the denial and other harm he hears from them, by turning to the Most High Presence and awaiting His help, He followed this with consolation through the allusion contained in what He displayed, by depicting for him the Day of their calamity and bringing it near, to the point that in the time of the revelation of this verse he hears what awaits them of punishments (mathulat) and calamitous disasters (qawari' al-musibat), as a warning to them and as good news to His allies of the completeness of His support over them and His victory for them in this world and the Hereafter. So He said: ﴿And listen﴾, i.e., listen by deliberately giving hearing your utmost effort, by lending your ear and turning your heart, after your glorification with praise, to what is said to them ﴿on the day the Caller calls﴾ to them in this world on the Day of Badr, the first of the days in which Allah manifested His glory for His allies through avenging Himself on their enemies, and in the Hereafter on the Day of Resurrection, in the form of the Second Blast and what follows it.

Since the purpose is to display greatness by depicting the completeness of power, and this is realized by making the distant hear from the place of the caller just as the near one hears, equally, and since nearness is necessarily tied to hearing, He said, depicting this: ﴿from a near place﴾, which is the rock of Bayt al-Maqdis, i.e., the one far away hears the voice just as the one nearby hears it; they are equal in their places, with no difference between them at all.

When he magnified this station by clothing it in the garment of generality (ijmal), he replaced that generality with clarification and added further magnification by saying: ﴿The day they hear﴾, meaning those who are called, ﴿the Cry﴾, meaning a cry that struck them deaf, namely the cry by which the one who summoned them to Badr in this world (al-Badr, the place of battle) rallied them. It was a cry that decreed their deafness to all their dealings. The cry of the second blast of the trumpet (al-Ṣūr) in the Hereafter is also meant. These are the two blasts of gathering (nafkhatā ḥashr) toward the judgment between the one who is in the right and the one who is in the wrong.

﴿In truth﴾, meaning the established matter that they used to call magic and regarded as imagination. Then they will know at that time that reality corresponds to it. It was therefore true, since reality has corresponded to it, and so reporting it was truthful.

When He, glorified be He, magnified it with generality after generality, indicating that what it contains of severe terrors would require lengthy explanation in speech, He increased its magnification by what this discourse produced, and said: ﴿That﴾, meaning the great day on which the striver is made manifest and the glory of the weak believers is raised, ﴿is the Day of Coming Forth﴾, meaning the day than which there is no greater coming forth. It is their coming forth from their houses in this world to their places of slaughter at Badr, and from their graves out of the earth from which they were created to their places of punishment in the Fire.

Now the Passage, "When the pillars of power were built and the glad tidings of victory were struck, and it was concluded with what applies to the resurrection, which is the greatest giving of life, indicating it by what is witnessed of His actions, and He emphasized it because of their denial of the resurrection, He said: ﴿Indeed We﴾, that is, with what belongs to Us of greatness, ﴿We alone﴾ ﴿give life and cause death﴾, this renewal of it, one thing after another, being a settled custom and a continuing habit as you witness it; for from Us was the beginning with the first giving of life. ﴿And to Us﴾, exclusively, is ﴿the final return﴾, that is, the becoming and its place and its time, by Our giving life to all whom We caused to die on the Day of Resurrection and gathering them to the place of judgment, then We judge (p-442) between them. The return is no harder than the origin. So whoever affirms this and denies the resurrection is, decisively, either a stubborn opponent or a madman.

Now that the matter of the Resurrection had been established with complete certainty, He depicted their coming forth in it, saying, linking it to what He had concluded the beginning of the passage with, for added magnification, exaltation and honoring: ﴿On the Day the earth splits asunder from them﴾. He expressed it with the verb of intransitive reflexive form (fi'l al-muṭāwaʿah) because the situation calls for it, and He omitted the reflexive taʾ (of tashaqqaqa) to indicate the ease of the action and its swiftness. ﴿From them﴾, meaning: passing over them, after they had been in its belly, so they come forth from it alive just as they were upon its surface alive, while they are ﴿hastening﴾ to answer its caller. He indicated its magnitude by His saying: ﴿That﴾, meaning: this bringing forth which is very great indeed, ﴿is a gathering﴾, meaning: a assembling under compulsion. He increased the explanation of the greatness of this matter by indicating its exclusivity through the fronting of the prepositional phrase, saying: ﴿upon Us﴾, meaning: exclusively, ﴿is easy﴾. How, then, could any rational person hesitate about it, let alone deny it, while for anyone other than Us it is not possible by any means? End of quotation.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (*Nazm al-Durar*) on surah 50, verse 45:

When He, glorified is He, had established the proofs of His complete power and the all-encompassing reach of His knowledge, and concluded them with His ease over it and His exclusive ownership of it, He connected to them a consolation for the Prophet (ﷺ), by threatening those who denied Him with the knowledge that is the greatest threat. So He said: ﴿We [alone]﴾, meaning: not other than Us, nor they themselves, ﴿are most knowing﴾, meaning: more than anyone who might be imagined to have knowledge, ﴿of what they say﴾, meaning: in the present and the future, of their denial of the Resurrection and other things, along with their acknowledgment of Our power.

Since the implied sense is: "We are able to restrain them from it by the all-encompassing knowledge We possess, and you are a warner to them, warning them of the consequence of that," He followed this with His saying: ﴿And you are not over them﴾ (p-٤٤٣). Since the particle of elevation (*harf al-isti'la'*, "over") conveys domination and overpowering, He emphasized the negation of it, saying: ﴿a tyrant﴾, meaning: an arrogant, overpowering, insolent one who forcibly turns them back from what you dislike of their sayings and deeds. ﴿You are only a warner.﴾ Having negated tyranny from him, He affirmed for them what the conjunctive *waw* had implied of warning, as I have estimated before it. So He said, as a consequence of it, using the word "remind," which arises from forgetfulness, because everything in the Qur'an that is admonition, when a person reflects upon it, he finds it witnessed within himself or in what he knows of the horizons: ﴿So remind﴾, meaning: by way of glad tidings and warning, ﴿with the Qur'an﴾, meaning: the one that gathers in its glory every good and encompasses every righteousness, ﴿whoever fears My threat﴾, meaning: whoever it is possible for to fear, which is every intelligent person. However, He phrased it this way to inform that the one who truly fears, so that his condition reveals his Islam, is the one intended in essence, while others are addressed only to establish the proof against them, not out of obstinacy on their part, and one should not grieve over them, nor be affected by their denial. Rather, one believes that they are nonexistent, whose enmity does no harm and whose allegiance brings no benefit, and they harm none but themselves and everyone who allies with them in this world and the Hereafter. This is the glory of the Qur'an, of the One who sent it down, and of the one who brought it, with complete power from Him, whose attribute is that and whose knowledge is all-encompassing. Thus this latter [passage] has been joined to that first [passage] with the utmost inclination, and its branches have wrapped around its root with the most complete enfolding. So it is acknowledged by [those of] eminence and by the people of fairness and of attributes of [precedence] in every craft, through a precedence whose overtaking is impossible, with every acknowledgment. And Allah is the Guide to what is correct.
